readings.title: The Little Girl with the Light
readings.challenge: Work out what the girl’s “light” is, since it is never a lamp or a candle.
readings.focus: Goodness and courage pictured as a light that changes how everyone else sees and acts.
readings.context: From Maud Lindsay’s Mother Stories, a book of tales for mothers to tell young children. The book prints a short motto for the mother before each story; it is left out here. A maiden is a girl. To flee is to run away. A dell is a small valley in the woods. Tanglewood is thick, tangled undergrowth.
readings.contentNote: Enemies seize the palace and imprison the king and queen, and a lost child walks alone through a dark forest past hunters and wild animals that want to harm her. Nothing harms her, and her father finds her in the morning.

excerpt.locator: “The Little Girl with the Light,” the whole story without the motto for the mother printed before it; opens “There once lived a little maiden to whom God had given a wonderful light, which made her…”; closes “…creatures she gave love and protection, and she lived happily all the days of her life.”.

questions.prompt: Where does the girl’s light show? Find two places.
facilitatorNotes: In her smile as a baby, in her eyes like sunshine, and on her forehead like a star. The story repeats the sunshine-and-star words later, in the forest.
evidence: it lighted up her eyes like sunshine, and gleamed on her forehead like a star

questions.prompt: In the forest she sees a giant waiting by the path. What is it really, and what does her light change?
facilitatorNotes: Only a pine tree with “friendly arms.” Seeing clearly turns her fear into laughter, and the woods laugh with her.
evidence: it was only a pine tree, stretching out its friendly arms

questions.prompt: The rabbit will not come to the palace. Why does it want to go home, and why does she let it?
facilitatorNotes: Its babies are waiting and it has work to do. She loves it enough to let it go; caring for someone does not always mean keeping them.
evidence: So the child kissed it and bade it go

questions.prompt: What do you think the light stands for? Use something she does to explain.
facilitatorNotes: Kindness, goodness, courage or love are all defensible. Ask the child to tie the answer to an action: not being afraid, sheltering the rabbit, or ruling kindly when she grows up.
evidence: But she was not afraid,—no! not even when she came to a great forest, at evening;—for she carried her light with her.

readings.title: The Open Gate — out into the world
readings.challenge: Notice how the farm animals talk like neighbours, and find the first sign of trouble.
readings.focus: Freedom looks wonderful to the brown colt until it begins to hurt.
readings.context: From Maud Lindsay’s Mother Stories, a book of tales for mothers to tell young children. The book prints a short motto for the mother before each story; it is left out here. A colt is a young horse. Brindle means brown with darker streaks. A threshing machine separates grain from straw, and the old steam ones had a loud whistle. Barbs are the sharp points on a wire fence.
readings.contentNote: The frightened colt jumps a barbed-wire fence and cuts himself.

excerpt.locator: “The Open Gate,” from the start of the story, after the motto for the mother, to the colt’s wish to see Dick; opens “One bright summer afternoon, Fleet, the good old shepherd dog that helped to take care of…”; closes “…and cut his feet as he leaped awkwardly over, "Oh! how I wish I could see Dick now."”.

questions.prompt: Before the trouble, what makes Fleet bark “with satisfaction”?
facilitatorNotes: Everything on the farm is in its place: hens in the dust, the calf asleep, ducks at the pond, horses at work. It is all calm.

questions.prompt: What do the three geese say has happened? How can you tell they are excited?
facilitatorNotes: The gate is open, the colt is gone, the calf is going, and they are “thinking about it”; they say it all in one breath and end with a honk.
evidence: The gate is open, the brown colt's gone, the brindle calf's going and we are thinking about it; quawk! quawk!

questions.prompt: Why does the colt shout “Hurrah!”? Does he know what it means?
facilitatorNotes: He copies Dick; he does not know the word, but he feels free and excited.
evidence: not because he knew what it meant but because he had heard Dick say it

questions.prompt: What changes the colt’s mind about being free?
facilitatorNotes: A loud whistle frightens him over a barbed fence; he tears his coat and cuts his feet, and wishes he could see Dick.
evidence: Oh! how I wish I could see Dick now.

readings.title: The Open Gate — the way home
readings.challenge: Find out who left the gate open, and notice how the boy and the colt are alike.
readings.focus: Carelessness has a cost, and both Dick and the colt come home changed.
readings.context: Recap: someone left the farmyard gate open, and the brown colt ran away. He loved his freedom until a loud whistle frightened him over a barbed-wire fence. Now the story goes back to the farm. A pike road is a main road. A cotton field grows cotton plants.

excerpt.locator: “The Open Gate,” from Dick at home to the end of the story; opens “But Dick was at home. He had run after the brown colt as fast as his feet could carry…”; closes “…them will ever forget the day when Dick was careless and did not shut the farmyard gate.”.

questions.prompt: Who left the gate open? What does Father say about it?
facilitatorNotes: Dick himself. Father says everyone, big or small, must take care of the things they want to keep.
evidence: for he was the very one who had forgotten to shut the farmyard gate
big boys and little boys and everybody else must take care of the things they wanted to keep

questions.prompt: Find two ways the colt and Dick are alike in this part of the story.
facilitatorNotes: Both hang their heads, and both think about each other all night. Both are sorry.
evidence: But the brown colt hung his head, as Dick had done

questions.prompt: The birds ask, “Is this the same brown colt that raised such a dust yesterday?” What do they mean?
facilitatorNotes: Yesterday he galloped proudly; today he limps home slowly. They notice how much he has changed.
evidence: Is this the same brown colt that raised such a dust yesterday?

questions.prompt: Dick and Fleet ask the colt no questions “because they understood.” What did they understand?
facilitatorNotes: That he was sorry and glad to be home, the way Dick was sorry. Some children may say they understood he was hurt; that fits too.
evidence: Dick and Friend Fleet asked no questions, because they understood
